title: What drives employment trends among older workers? (Economic Bulletin, Issue 3/2026)
key_claim: The euro-area rise in labour force participation since 2019 has been most pronounced among older workers (and women); the current trend toward later retirement is a key driver of employment growth, with the participation rate of the 55-74 age group rising markedly and later exit from the labour market accounting for much of the gain.
frame_summary: The ECB argues later retirement and higher older-worker participation are a primary, quantified driver of euro-area labour supply growth, not a marginal effect.

title: Drivers of the labour force in the euro area (Economic Bulletin, Issue 3/2026)
date_evidence: ECB Economic Bulletin Issue 3/2026, published 13 May 2026 (same issue as box ebbox202603_05, meta published_time 2026-05-13)
key_claim: The euro-area labour force has kept growing despite population ageing, with participation gains concentrated among older workers and women; the participation rate for the 55-74 age group rose from about 40.3% in Q4 2019 to 44.9% in Q4 2025, cushioning the demographic drag on labour supply.
frame_summary: The ECB frames rising participation, led by older workers, as the main force keeping euro-area labour supply growing against demographic headwinds.

title: Transition to State Pension age (inquiry, oral evidence)
date_evidence: UK Parliament Work and Pensions Committee, 'Transition to State Pension age' inquiry, oral evidence 18 March 2026 (committees.parliament.uk/event/26759)
key_claim: The UK State Pension age began rising from 66 toward 67 in April 2026 (phased to 2028), and Parliament's Work and Pensions Committee is examining the transition, including the risk that many people are already out of the labour market before pension age and the case for stronger support to keep older workers economically active.
frame_summary: The Committee frames the pension-age rise as institutionalising longer working lives while warning that policy must actively keep older workers in the labour market for the lever to pay off.

title: Ageing and employment
date_evidence: Evergreen OECD topic page (Ageing and employment); accessed 2026-07-12
key_claim: The OECD holds that mobilising untapped labour, especially older workers (and women), is key to offsetting demographic decline and sustaining living standards, and that improving opportunities and conditions for older workers supports both pension sustainability and labour supply.
frame_summary: The OECD frames older-worker mobilisation as a central policy lever for offsetting ageing, alongside (not only) migration.

title: Bosses Are Snubbing Younger Workers for 50-Year-Olds
date_evidence: meta article:published_time 2026-06-24T16:47:16+01:00; byline 'Published 24 June 2026, 4:47 PM BST'
